why: Each guest ordered exactly one dish, so the total is 12 + 9 = 21. Three is the difference between the groups, not the total.

q: Four friends took a quiz. Nia scored higher than Oscar. Pablo scored lower than Oscar. Quinn scored higher than Nia. Who scored lowest?
why: From the clues, the order from highest to lowest is Quinn, Nia, Oscar, Pablo, so Pablo is lowest. Oscar is below Nia but above Pablo.

q: One of three boxes holds a prize. Box 1 says, “The prize is here.” Box 2 says, “The prize is not here.” Box 3 says, “The prize is not in Box 1.” Exactly one label is true. Where is the prize?
why: If the prize were in Box 1, labels 1 and 2 would both be true; if in Box 3, labels 2 and 3 would both be true. Only with the prize in Box 2 is exactly one label (Box 3’s) true.

q: All of the runners on the school team are students. Some students at the school play chess. Which must be true?
options: Nothing certain follows about whether any runner plays chess.
why: The chess-playing students could all be people who are not runners, so we can’t conclude that any runner plays chess. “Some runners play chess” sounds natural but does not have to be true.

q: Passing the final exam is necessary to pass the course. Elif passed the final exam. Which must be true?
options: Elif may or may not have passed the course.
Everyone who passed the final passed the course.
Elif did not need to pass the final.
why: A necessary condition must be met, but meeting it may not be enough; Elif might have failed other parts of the course. Concluding she passed treats necessary as if it meant sufficient.

q: Kai is two years older than Lea. Lea is three years younger than Max. Max is 20. How old is Kai?
why: Lea is 3 years younger than Max, so she is 17; Kai is 2 years older than Lea, so he is 19. Seventeen is Lea’s age, not Kai’s.

q: Which word is most nearly the OPPOSITE of optimistic?
why: Optimistic means expecting things to turn out well; pessimistic means expecting them to turn out badly. Realistic is sometimes set against optimistic, but it means seeing things as they are, not expecting the worst.

q: Which word is most nearly the OPPOSITE of temporary?
why: Temporary means lasting only for a while; permanent means lasting for good. Brief is close in meaning to temporary, not its opposite.

q: Which word is most nearly the OPPOSITE of humble?
why: Humble means not thinking you are better than others; arrogant means acting as if you are. Modest is a synonym, and rude is about bad manners, not pride.

q: Which word is closest in meaning to diligent?
why: Diligent means putting steady care and effort into work, which is what hardworking means. Intelligent describes ability, not effort; lazy is the opposite.

q: Which word is closest in meaning to hostile?
why: Hostile means unfriendly and ready to oppose or attack. A strict person sets firm rules but is not necessarily unfriendly.

q: Which word is closest in meaning to ambiguous?
why: Ambiguous means open to more than one meaning, so it is unclear. Something complicated can still have one clear meaning, and ambitious only sounds similar.

q: Which is the odd one out? delighted, thrilled, overjoyed, elated, dismayed, ecstatic
why: All the others mean very happy; dismayed means upset and discouraged. Ecstatic is the strongest of the happy words, but it is still a happy word.

q: Which is the odd one out? hurricane, tornado, blizzard, earthquake, typhoon, monsoon
why: All the others are kinds of weather: storms, or seasonal winds and rains, in the air. An earthquake is a shaking of the ground caused by movement of rock deep underground. A monsoon is a seasonal wind that brings months of heavy rain, so it is weather too.

def: believing something is true because you want it to be true, not because the evidence shows it
scenario: Tomás hasn’t practiced for his driving test, but he’s sure he’ll pass because he really wants to drive to the beach this weekend.
fix: Ask yourself what the evidence would say if you didn’t care how things turned out.

tests.s: Aisha keeps telling herself the grinding noise in her car will go away on its own, simply because she can’t afford a repair right now.
Wei is certain his lost wallet will be returned with all the cash inside, only because he can’t bear to think otherwise.

def: excusing a bad action by saying it is fine because someone else did something bad first
scenario: After a driver cuts her off, Hannah speeds up and cuts him off in return, insisting he had it coming.
fix: Judge each action on its own; another person’s wrong doesn’t make yours acceptable.
note: Not the same as tu quoque, which brushes off a criticism because the critic does the same thing.

tests.s: Liam admits he copied a classmate’s essay, but says it’s fair because that classmate once took credit for one of his ideas.
Because a store overcharged Sofia last month, she decides it’s fine to walk out today without paying for a candy bar.

def: judging a person or idea as bad because of the people or groups connected to it
scenario: Jamal’s coworkers start avoiding him after learning his roommate was fired for stealing, though Jamal had nothing to do with it.
fix: Ask what the person or idea itself has done or shown, apart from who it is linked to.

tests.s: A parent won’t let her son join the chess club because one of its members was once caught shoplifting.
Residents are urged to reject a new park plan simply because a company that once polluted the river also supports it.

def: treating a claim as wrong by mocking it or making it sound silly, without giving any real reasons
scenario: When Priya suggests the office try a four-day week, her manager snorts, “That’s the funniest thing I’ve heard all year,” and the meeting moves on without discussing it.
fix: Notice when laughter takes the place of reasons, and ask what is actually wrong with the idea.
note: Unlike ad hominem, the mockery is aimed at the idea rather than at the person.

tests.s: At a town meeting, Kwame proposes bike lanes; a resident rolls his eyes and says, “Oh, how adorable,” people chuckle, and no one gives a reason against the lanes.
Instead of answering Elena’s case for a later school start time, a columnist just calls it “a bedtime story for grown-ups” and moves on.

def: the difference between a statement that can be checked and shown true or false and a personal view or judgment
scenario: A town website says, “Our lake is 40 feet deep, and it’s the prettiest spot in the county.” The depth can be measured; “prettiest” is a matter of taste.
fix: Ask whether a statement could be checked with evidence, or whether it depends on someone’s tastes and values.

tests.s: Malik tells his sister she is simply wrong to prefer jazz, because rock is the better kind of music, “and that’s just a fact.”
A phone review presents “the most beautiful phone ever made” as a proven truth, right next to its measured battery life of 20 hours.

def: the habit of crediting your successes to your own skill while blaming your failures on bad luck or other people
scenario: When her team wins, Fatima says it was her great coaching; when they lose, she blames the referees.
fix: Explain your wins and losses the same way, and look honestly at what was in your control both times.

tests.s: Diego says he aced the history exam because he’s smart, but that he failed the chemistry exam because the teacher wrote unfair questions.
A store manager credits a record sales month to her own display ideas, then blames the weather when sales drop the next month.

def: using a small piece of someone’s words in a way that changes or hides what they actually meant
scenario: A critic writes, “This film is far from a masterpiece,” and the movie’s poster quotes him as calling it “a masterpiece.”
fix: Find the full original statement and check whether the quote still means the same thing in its setting.

tests.s: A school newsletter reports that the principal said “homework should be doubled,” leaving out that her full sentence was “Some parents say homework should be doubled, but I disagree.”
Rosa’s review says, “The hotel would be great if not for the noise and the rude staff,” and the hotel’s website quotes her as saying, “The hotel would be great.”

def: a situation where the person judging, studying or advising has something to gain from one particular answer
scenario: A study praising a new energy drink turns out to have been paid for and run by the company that makes it.
fix: Ask who paid for or benefits from a claim, and look for checks by people with nothing to gain.
note: Having one doesn’t prove a claim is false; it is a reason to check the claim more carefully.

tests.s: A judge at a baking contest awards first prize to an entry without mentioning that the baker is her own daughter.
A financial adviser urges Olga to buy a fund but doesn’t tell her he earns a bonus for every customer he signs up for it.

def: the tendency to give bad news, criticism or bad experiences more weight than equally strong good ones
scenario: Yuki gets ten warm compliments on her presentation and one critical comment, and the criticism is all she can think about that night.
fix: Count the good and the bad on purpose, and ask whether one bad item really outweighs all the rest.

tests.s: After one rude waiter on the last evening, Hannah remembers her whole week-long trip as a disaster, though every other day was wonderful.
Jamal’s performance review is full of praise plus one small suggestion, and he spends the evening convinced his boss thinks he’s failing.

def: a single case that shows a general claim, such as one using “all” or “never,” is false
scenario: Aisha’s brother claims no bird can swim underwater. She points to penguins, which dive for fish, and his claim falls apart.
fix: When you hear “all,” “every” or “never,” look for just one case that breaks the rule.

tests.s: Diego claims every prime number is odd, and his teacher simply writes the number 2 on the board.
Wei insists all mammals give birth to live young, until his daughter shows him a picture of a platypus laying eggs.

def: arguing that two things alike in some ways must also be alike in another important way, when they are not
scenario: “A company is like a family,” the owner says, “so employees shouldn’t expect to be paid for staying late.”
fix: List the important ways the two things differ, and check whether those differences affect the conclusion.

tests.s: “Students are like customers, and the customer is always right,” Liam argues, “so teachers should never give a grade a student disagrees with.”
“Learning to code is just like learning to ride a bike,” Omar says, “so once you learn one programming language, you’ll never need to study again.”

def: assuming that something is better or more correct simply because it is new or modern
scenario: Hannah replaces her reliable laptop the day a new model comes out, saying the newest one must be better, without checking a single review.
fix: Ask what actual improvement the new thing offers, apart from being recent.
note: The reverse of appeal to tradition, which favors something because it is old.

tests.s: A school drops a reading program that was working well because the principal says a program released this year must be more effective.
A diet ad claims its plan beats all others because it is “the latest discovery,” and offers no other evidence.

def: deciding a claim must be false because you personally find it hard to believe or imagine
scenario: “I just can’t imagine how a metal plane that heavy stays in the air,” says Olga, “so I don’t believe the engineers’ explanation.”
fix: Remember that how hard something is to picture tells you about your own knowledge, not about the facts.

tests.s: Kwame says he can’t see how ancient builders moved such huge stones with simple tools, so they must have used some lost, advanced technology.
Priya refuses to accept that the light from some stars left them thousands of years ago, because the idea seems too strange to be true.

def: the tendency to favor and trust people who belong to your own group over those who don’t
scenario: Judging a science fair, a teacher gives slightly higher scores to projects from her own school than to equally good projects from other schools.
fix: Judge people by the same standard you would want used on your own group, and hide group labels when you can.

tests.s: A hiring manager rates candidates from his own old college as “sharper,” even when their interviews were no better than anyone else’s.
Fans call their own team’s rough tackles “tough, hard-nosed play” but call the very same tackles by rival players “dirty.”

def: the tendency to think far more people share your own opinions, habits and choices than really do
scenario: Malik is sure nearly everyone at work wants a later start time like he does, and is shocked when most coworkers vote to keep it the same.
fix: Ask others directly, or look at real survey data, instead of assuming they think as you do.

tests.s: Sofia, who dislikes parties, assumes almost every guest at the party is secretly wishing they could go home early.
Because Tomás loves spicy food, he plans a dinner where every dish is very hot, assuming most of his guests will love it too.

def: the tendency to believe other people notice your looks or mistakes far more than they actually do
scenario: Jamal spills coffee on his shirt before a meeting and spends the hour sure everyone is staring at the stain; afterward, no one remembers it.
fix: Remember that most people are busy thinking about themselves, and ask a friend what they actually noticed.

tests.s: After stumbling over one word in her toast, Fatima is convinced the whole wedding is talking about it, though no guest even noticed.
Liam wears mismatched socks to class and spends the day hiding his feet, certain that everyone has seen them.

def: the tendency to believe you are less likely than other people to face bad events such as illness, accidents or failure
scenario: Aisha knows many new restaurants close within a few years, but she’s sure hers won’t, so she saves no money for a slow first year.
fix: Start with how often things go wrong for people in your situation, then ask what truly makes your case different.

tests.s: Diego knows texting while driving causes many crashes, but he believes he is careful enough that it won’t happen to him.
At a workshop, nearly every newlywed couple says their own chance of divorce is close to zero, though they know many marriages end in divorce.

def: an idea an argument depends on but never states, which must be true for the conclusion to follow
scenario: “We should hire Elena; she has the most years of experience,” says the manager, quietly assuming experience matters more than anything else for the job.
fix: Ask what else would have to be true for the conclusion to follow, and then check whether it is.

tests.s: Rosa argues, “The new bus route is faster, so more people will ride it,” which only works if speed is the main reason people avoid the bus.
“Kwame scored the most points, so he’s our most valuable player,” a fan says, taking for granted that scoring is all that makes a player valuable.

def: the difference between original evidence, such as a study, letter or recording, and a later report or summary of it
scenario: A news story says a study found coffee “doubles” memory, but the study itself reports only a small improvement on one memory test.
fix: When a claim matters, trace it back to the original document or data, not just a report about it.

tests.s: Priya’s essay quotes a website’s summary of a famous speech, and she later finds the actual recording, where the speaker’s words are quite different.
A rumor says the new city budget cuts all library funding, but the budget document itself shows a 3% reduction.

def: the belief that you can influence results that are really decided by chance
scenario: Malik always picks his own lottery numbers instead of random ones, convinced that choosing them himself improves his odds.
fix: Ask whether anything you do could actually change the result; if not, the outcome is luck.

tests.s: At game night, Hannah blows on the dice and throws them extra hard whenever she needs a high number.
Jamal presses the crosswalk button again and again, sure it makes the light change faster, though the light runs on a fixed timer.

def: the statement “if not B, then not A,” which is always true whenever “if A, then B” is true
scenario: “If you live in Chicago, you live in Illinois” means the same as “If you don’t live in Illinois, you don’t live in Chicago.”
fix: To restate an if-then rule safely, swap the two parts and make both negative; just swapping them makes a different claim.
note: Not the same as the converse (“if B, then A”), which does not follow from the original statement.

tests.s: Every guest with a wristband was checked at the door. So Yuki reasons that any guest who wasn’t checked at the door can’t have a wristband.
Knowing that the game is canceled whenever it rains, Malik hears the game was not canceled and correctly concludes it did not rain.

def: a test in which neither the people taking part nor the researchers working with them know who gets the real treatment
scenario: In a pain-relief trial, pills are coded by number so that neither the patients nor the nurses know which are real medicine and which are sugar pills.
fix: Ask whether anyone’s expectations could have shaped the results; good studies keep both sides in the dark.
note: In a single-blind study, usually only the participants don’t know which treatment they are getting.

tests.s: In a study of a new allergy spray, neither the volunteers nor the doctors examining them are told which sprays contain the medicine until all results are in.
A coffee taste test hides the brand names from the tasters, and the staff serving the cups don’t know which brand is which either.

def: the difficulty experts have in imagining what it is like not to know what they know, so they explain things poorly
scenario: A software engineer tells a new coworker from the sales team to “just clear the cache and update the browser,” not realizing those words mean nothing to him.
fix: Explain things to an imagined beginner, and check understanding by asking the listener to say it back in their own words.

tests.s: A math professor skips steps in his lecture because they seem obvious to him, leaving most first-year students lost.
A chef writes a recipe that just says “make a roux,” forgetting that most home cooks don’t know what that means.

def: the belief that people generally get what they deserve, so those who suffer must have done something to cause it
scenario: When a hardworking neighbor loses her job in a citywide factory closing, Olga says she must have done something wrong, because “good people don’t end up unemployed.”
fix: Remember that luck, timing and forces outside a person’s control shape many outcomes.

tests.s: After a storm floods a whole street, a passerby says the families there must have deserved it somehow, since “life punishes people who don’t live right.”
Hearing that a stranger was cheated out of his savings, Diego insists the man must have been greedy, because honest people get what they deserve.

def: accepting vague statements that could fit almost anyone as a surprisingly accurate description of yourself
scenario: Sofia reads a horoscope saying she “sometimes doubts herself but shows strength when it counts” and feels it describes her perfectly.
fix: Ask whether the description would fit most of your friends just as well; if so, it says nothing special about you.
note: Also called the Forer effect, after psychologist Bertram Forer, who gave students the same “personal” profile and found most rated it highly accurate.

tests.s: After an online quiz tells him he “values close friends but also needs time alone,” Kwame decides the quiz truly understands his personality.
A palm reader tells Elena she “has a creative side she doesn’t always show,” and Elena is amazed at how well the reader knows her.

def: real unpleasant symptoms that people feel because they expect something to harm them, even when it is fake or harmless
scenario: In a drug trial, many people taking sugar pills report headaches and nausea after reading the list of possible side effects.
fix: Compare side effects in the real-treatment group with those in a sugar-pill group before blaming the treatment.
note: The negative twin of the placebo effect. Nocebo is Latin for “I will harm.”

tests.s: Told that a harmless wristband might cause dizziness, several volunteers start to feel dizzy within minutes of putting it on.
After hearing that a new cell tower could cause headaches, residents report more headaches, even though the tower hasn’t been switched on yet.

def: judging whether a decision was good by how it turned out, rather than by what was known when it was made
scenario: Tomás drives home after a long night with almost no sleep and arrives safely, so he decides it was a fine choice.
fix: Ask whether the decision made sense with the information available at the time, whatever happened afterward.

tests.s: Fatima puts all her savings into one risky stock; it soars, and her friends praise her for making a wise financial decision.
A coach makes a sensible, well-planned call late in the game, but when a freak bounce costs his team the win, fans say it was a terrible decision.

def: describing the other side’s argument in its strongest, most reasonable form before you respond to it
scenario: Before arguing against a later school start, Hannah says, “The best case for it is that teens would get more sleep and might earn better grades. Here’s why I still disagree.”
fix: Before you disagree, ask whether the other side would say you described their view fairly, or even better than they did.
note: The opposite of a straw man, which makes the other side’s view weaker than it really is.

tests.s: Kwame wants to keep the open-plan office, but first he lays out the strongest reasons for private offices, including points his coworkers hadn’t thought of.
Yuki opens the debate by stating her opponent’s case so fairly that her opponent says, “Yes, that’s exactly my view, and better than I put it.”

def: giving a number in more exact detail than the evidence can support, which makes a rough guess look certain
scenario: A town website reports that exactly 10,483 people attended the festival, though organizers only glanced at the crowd and guessed.
fix: Ask how the number was measured, and round it to what that method can honestly support.

tests.s: A weather forecaster announces that next Tuesday’s high will be 71.36 degrees, as if a forecast could be that exact.
An ad claims its cream makes skin look 27.4% younger, based on a handful of people judging photos by eye.

def: believing that a specific combination of events is more likely than just one of those events on its own
scenario: Told that Jae is quiet and loves books, many people rate “Jae is a librarian who writes poetry” as more likely than “Jae is a librarian,” though it can’t be.
fix: Remember that each added detail can only keep the odds the same or lower them, never raise them.
note: Made famous by Amos Tversky and Daniel Kahneman’s “Linda problem.”

tests.s: Priya says it’s more likely that a team will “lose its star player to injury and then miss the playoffs” than simply that it will “miss the playoffs.”
Diego thinks his flight is more likely to be “delayed by a snowstorm” than just “delayed,” because the storm makes the story feel real.

q: numismatist : coins :: philatelist : ?
why: A numismatist collects and studies coins; a philatelist collects and studies postage stamps. Old books are the interest of a bibliophile, a different kind of collector.

q: archipelago : island :: constellation : ?
why: An archipelago is a group of islands, and a constellation is a group of stars. A galaxy is also made of stars, but it is a whole group, not a single member.

q: kiln : potter :: forge : ?
why: A potter fires clay in a kiln, and a blacksmith heats metal in a forge; each is the worker’s furnace. An anvil is another blacksmith’s tool, not the worker who uses the forge.

q: illegible : read :: inaudible : ?
why: Something illegible can’t be read, and something inaudible can’t be heard. Whisper is tempting because whispers can be hard to hear, but it isn’t the action that fails.

q: census : population :: inventory : ?
why: A census is an official count of a population, and an inventory is a count of the goods a business has in stock. The warehouse is where the goods are kept, not what is counted.

q: miser : money :: glutton : ?
why: A miser has an excessive desire to hold on to money, and a glutton has an excessive desire for food. Hunger is a feeling a glutton may have, not the thing wanted to excess.

q: seismologist : earthquakes :: meteorologist : ?
why: A seismologist studies earthquakes, and a meteorologist studies weather. Despite the name, meteorologists do not study meteors; astronomers do.

q: verbose : terse :: lavish : ?
why: Verbose (using too many words) is the opposite of terse (using very few), and lavish (spending freely) is the opposite of frugal (spending carefully). Luxurious is close in meaning to lavish, not its opposite.

q: “After the mill closed, the family lived a penurious life, stretching one bag of rice across a week and patching the same coats every winter.” What does penurious most likely mean?
why: Losing their income, rationing food and mending old coats all point to deep poverty. The family may also be unhappy, but nothing in the sentence describes their feelings.

q: “A sedulous researcher, Amara checked each of the 4,000 records by hand, twice, before she would publish a single number.” What does sedulous most likely mean?
why: Checking thousands of records by hand, twice, shows steady, careful effort. Someone that thorough might seem slow, but nothing suggests she is slow to understand.

q: “The volcano has been quiescent for two centuries, but scientists warn that it could erupt again.” What does quiescent most likely mean?
why: The volcano has done nothing for 200 years yet could erupt again, so it is resting, not finished. “Permanently dead” is ruled out by the warning that it could erupt.

q: “Living an ascetic life, the monk owned one robe and one bowl and slept on a bare wooden floor.” What does ascetic most likely mean?
options: simple and without comforts, by choice
why: Owning almost nothing and sleeping on a bare floor show a chosen life without comforts. A monk may live alone, but the details describe self-denial, not loneliness.

q: “Sloths are arboreal animals, spending nearly their whole lives hanging from the branches of trees.” What does arboreal most likely mean?
why: The sentence explains the word by saying sloths live hanging in trees. Sloths are also slow, but the sentence ties the word to where they live, not how they move.

q: “The plaintive notes of the violin drifted across the hall, and several people in the audience quietly wiped their eyes.” What does plaintive most likely mean?
why: Listeners wiping tears suggests the music sounded sad. Out-of-tune notes might make people wince, but they would not move an audience to tears.

q: “The farmer left the east field fallow this year, plowing it but planting nothing so the soil could recover.” What does fallow most likely mean?
options: plowed but left unplanted for a season
why: The sentence says the field was plowed but nothing was planted, so the soil could rest. A resting field may grow weeds, but the word refers to leaving it unplanted on purpose.

q: “The hotel put a latch high on the door after a guest, a somnambulist, was found wandering the hallway at 3 a.m. with no memory of leaving her room.” What does somnambulist most likely mean?
options: a person who walks while asleep
a person who cannot fall asleep
a person who talks in their sleep
why: Wandering at night with no memory of it points to walking while asleep. Someone who cannot fall asleep would remember being awake and walking around.

q: In Brookfield, the number of bike accidents rose from 50 to 60 over five years. Over the same period, the number of people who bike regularly doubled. Which is best supported?
options: Biking in Brookfield became more dangerous.
The accident rate for each rider likely went down.
The new riders are less careful than the old ones.
Bike accidents will reach 70 within five years.
why: Accidents rose 20% while riders rose 100%, so there were fewer accidents per rider. The raw rise makes biking look more dangerous, but that ignores how many more people were riding.

q: In a class of 40 students, 25 play soccer, 22 play basketball, and 5 play neither sport. Which must be true?
options: At most 3 students play both sports.
More students play only basketball than only soccer.
why: Thirty-five students play at least one sport, but 25 + 22 = 47, so 47 − 35 = 12 are counted twice and play both. That leaves 13 who play only soccer, not 15.

q: Officials in Dunmore credit a new ban on idling trucks near schools for a 30% drop in children’s asthma visits to the emergency room last year. Which, if true, most strengthens their claim?
options: Over the same year, asthma visits stayed level in nearby towns that had no such ban.
Many parents in Dunmore support the ban.
Truck drivers in Dunmore dislike the ban.
Asthma visits in Dunmore had dropped about 30% in each of the three years before the ban.
The ban was widely reported on local news.
why: Similar towns without the ban saw no drop, which makes the ban a likelier cause. A steady 30% yearly drop before the ban would weaken the claim, since the trend began earlier.

q: After Route 9 was widened from two lanes to four, traffic jams on it got worse within two years, even though the town’s population did not grow. Which best explains this?
options: Widening a road always makes traffic worse.
The extra lanes drew drivers who used to take other roads or travel at other times.
Fewer people in the region own cars than before.
Most drivers on Route 9 travel alone.
The speed limit on Route 9 stayed the same.
why: A roomier road can attract drivers from other routes and times until it fills up again. “Always makes traffic worse” overstates the case, and population growth is ruled out by the passage.

q: At a 10-person startup, the average (mean) salary is $150,000. Nine of the employees each earn $60,000. Which must be true?
options: Most employees earn more than the average salary.
The company pays more than other startups.
why: Total pay is 10 × $150,000 = $1.5 million; the nine earn $540,000, leaving $960,000 for the tenth. $1.5 million is the total payroll, not one person’s salary.

q: Last year, 40% of Bramble Books’ sales were online. This year, 50% were online. Which is best supported?
options: Online sales grew in dollar terms.
In-store sales fell in dollar terms.
Online sales made up a larger share of sales, but these figures alone can’t show whether they grew in dollars.
Half of the store’s customers now shop online.
The store will be online-only within five years.
why: A bigger share can come from online sales growing or from total sales shrinking, so the dollar change is unknown. “Online sales grew” is tempting but would be false if total sales fell enough.

q: A survey found that people who use a popular sleep-tracking app report worse sleep than people who don’t. A blogger concludes that the app harms sleep. Which, if true, best explains the survey result without the app causing worse sleep?
options: The app is free to download.
Some people who use the app sleep well.
The app’s screen is very bright at night.
Many people have never used a sleep app.
People who already sleep poorly are more likely to download a sleep app.
Poor sleep is linked to heart disease.
why: If bad sleepers are the ones who seek out the app, the poor sleep comes first and the app use follows. A bright screen would support the blogger, since it suggests the app itself harms sleep.

q: In Millford, most residents oppose the new parking plan. Most of the residents who oppose it live downtown. Which must be true?
options: Most downtown residents oppose the plan.
Some downtown residents oppose the plan.
No one outside downtown opposes the plan.
More than half of downtown residents support the plan.
why: Since most opponents live downtown, at least some downtown residents must oppose it. “Most downtown residents oppose it” doesn’t follow: if downtown is very large, its opponents could still be a minority there.

q: At Lumen, every employee who works remotely attends the Monday video call. Some employees who attend the Monday call are managers. Nadia works at Lumen and does not attend the Monday call. Which must be true?
options: Nadia works remotely but missed this call.
why: Every remote worker attends, so anyone who doesn’t attend can’t be remote. “Nadia is not a manager” doesn’t follow, because nothing says all managers attend the call.

q: The city museum is free for city residents, and it is free for everyone on Tuesdays. No one is charged when admission is free. Kofi was charged admission at the museum. Which must be true?
options: Kofi is not a city resident, and he did not visit on a Tuesday.
Kofi is a city resident who visited on a Tuesday.
Kofi is not a city resident, but he may have visited on a Tuesday.
Nothing can be concluded about Kofi.
why: Either a residence or a Tuesday visit would have made his entry free, so both must be ruled out. Visiting on a weekend is possible but not required; any non-Tuesday would do.

q: Every flight that left from Gate 9 today departed late. Every flight that departed late today was run by Skyway Air. Which must be true?
options: Every Skyway Air flight today departed late.
Every flight from Gate 9 today was run by Skyway Air.
Some Skyway Air flights today left from other gates.
Every late flight today left from Gate 9.
At least one Skyway Air flight departed on time today.
Gate 9 is always used only by Skyway Air.
why: Gate 9 flights were all late, and all late flights were Skyway’s, so all Gate 9 flights were Skyway’s. “Every Skyway flight was late” reverses the second statement, which doesn’t follow.

q: Exactly one of three siblings, Amir, Bea and Cole, broke a vase. Amir says, “I didn’t do it.” Bea says, “Amir did it.” Cole says, “I didn’t do it.” Exactly one of these three statements is true. Who broke the vase?
options: Amir or Bea, but it can’t be told which
why: If Cole did it, only Amir’s statement is true, which fits. If Amir did it, Bea and Cole would both be telling the truth; if Bea did it, Amir and Cole would be.

q: Five boxes, P, Q, R, S and T, all have different weights. P is heavier than Q. S is heavier than P. Q is heavier than R. T is heavier than R but lighter than Q. Which box is the second lightest?
why: From heaviest to lightest the order must be S, P, Q, T, R, so T is second lightest. R is the lightest of all, which makes it the tempting wrong answer.

q: A team holds four meetings, Monday through Thursday, one per day: budget, hiring, sales and training. Sales is on Monday. Hiring is the day right after budget. Training is not on Thursday. On which day is the budget meeting?
why: Budget on Tuesday would put hiring on Wednesday and training on Thursday, which is not allowed. So budget is Wednesday, hiring Thursday, and training Tuesday.

q: The alarm sounds only if the door is opened while the system is armed. The alarm sounded at 2 a.m. Which must be true?
options: The door was opened while the system was armed.
Whenever the door is opened while the system is armed, the alarm sounds.
The system was armed, but the door may have stayed closed.
The door was opened, but the system may not have been armed.
Nothing follows unless we know who opened the door.
why: “Only if” states a requirement: since the alarm sounded, both conditions were met. The second option reverses the rule; the passage never says the alarm must sound whenever those conditions hold.

q: In a warehouse, every red box is heavy, some heavy boxes are fragile, and no fragile box is red. Which must be true?
options: Some heavy boxes are not red.
Some fragile boxes are not heavy.
Every heavy box that isn’t fragile is red.
why: The heavy boxes that are fragile can’t be red, so at least some heavy boxes are not red. Whether any fragile boxes are light is never stated, so “some fragile boxes are not heavy” doesn’t follow.

q: Which word is most similar in meaning to truncate?
why: To truncate is to shorten something by cutting off part of it, as in a truncated speech. Lengthen is its opposite, and translate and transfer only look similar.

q: Which word is most nearly the OPPOSITE of halcyon, as in “the halcyon days of our youth”?
why: Halcyon means calm, peaceful and happy, so turbulent, meaning full of disorder and conflict, is its opposite. Golden and peaceful are close in meaning, not opposite.

q: Which word is the odd one out? canine, feline, bovine, equine, saline, porcine
why: Canine, porcine, equine, feline and bovine describe animals (dogs, pigs, horses, cats and cattle). Saline means containing salt, despite its matching ending.

q: Which word is most nearly the OPPOSITE of hirsute?
why: Hirsute means very hairy, so hairless is its opposite. Hairy and shaggy are near synonyms, not opposites.

q: Which word is most nearly the OPPOSITE of diurnal, as used of animals?
why: A diurnal animal is active during the day; a nocturnal animal is active at night. Diurnal can also mean daily, so “daily” is a synonym trap, not an opposite.

q: Which choice is most similar in meaning to recumbent?
why: Recumbent means lying down, as in a recumbent bicycle ridden while leaning far back. “Returning often” describes recurrent, a look-alike word.

q: Which word is the odd one out? meandering, rambling, digressive, long-winded, wordy, pithy
why: Pithy means brief and full of meaning; all the others describe speech or writing that goes on too long or wanders off topic.

q: Which pair does NOT show the same relationship as the others?
why: In every other pair, a worker shapes a material into something. A hospital is where a surgeon works, not a material the surgeon shapes.

def: the idea that once people are judged by a number, it stops being a good measure of what it was meant to show
scenario: A hospital starts judging its emergency room by how fast patients are “seen.” Staff begin giving a quick hello at the door and counting that as seen, so wait times look shorter while real care is no faster.
fix: When a number becomes a target, look for ways people could raise the number without improving the thing it was meant to show.
note: Economist Charles Goodhart made the point in 1975; the popular wording “When a measure becomes a target, it ceases to be a good measure” comes from Marilyn Strathern (1997).

tests.s: A city pays police bonuses for lowering reported crime, and officers start writing up stolen bikes as “lost property,” so the crime figures fall while thefts don’t.
A software team is rewarded for the number of bugs it fixes each week, and programmers begin splitting single bugs into several small tickets to fix one by one.

def: making a bold, hard-to-defend claim, then retreating to a mild, obvious version when challenged, and later returning to the bold one
scenario: Wei tells friends that “all modern art is a scam.” When challenged, he says he only meant that some artworks sell for silly prices, which no one denies. The next week he is again calling all modern art a scam.
fix: Ask which claim the person is actually defending, and hold them to that one when they switch back.
note: Named by philosopher Nicholas Shackel in 2005, after a castle design: a raised, easily defended mound (the motte) beside a larger yard that is harder to defend (the bailey).

tests.s: A blogger writes that a popular diet “cures diabetes.” When doctors object, she says she only meant that eating more vegetables is healthy, then goes back to selling the diet as a cure.
Malik insists that astrology predicts your future. Questioned, he says he just means the sun and moon affect things like tides and seasons, but the next day he plans his week by his horoscope.

def: rejecting a real, useful solution because it is not perfect, by comparing it with an ideal that can never be reached
scenario: “Seat belts don’t prevent every death in a crash,” Olga argues, “so there’s no point in requiring them.”
fix: Compare the proposal with the real alternatives, including doing nothing, not with a flawless option that doesn’t exist.
note: Named by economist Harold Demsetz in 1969.

tests.s: A council member votes against a new recycling program because, even with it, some of the town’s waste would still end up in the landfill.
Diego refuses to use a password manager because no software can be made 100% safe from hackers, so he keeps reusing one password everywhere.

def: the principle that the more surprising a claim is, the stronger the evidence must be before we accept it
scenario: Priya believes her coworker when he says he had pancakes for breakfast, but when he says he saw a ghost in the break room, she wants much more than his word.
fix: Weigh the evidence against how likely the claim was to begin with; a claim that breaks well-tested knowledge needs proof strong enough to outweigh all of it.
note: Carl Sagan made the line “Extraordinary claims require extraordinary evidence” famous, notably on his 1980 TV series Cosmos; David Hume and Pierre-Simon Laplace made similar points earlier.

tests.s: A science journal accepts a routine finding based on one careful study, but when a lab claims a battery that never needs charging, the editors demand that other labs repeat the test first.
Hannah takes her neighbor’s word that the bakery has new hours, but when he says lemon water cured his cancer, she asks to see medical records and real studies.

def: noticing that a news source gets your own field badly wrong, yet still trusting it fully on every other subject
scenario: Tomás, an airline pilot, laughs at a magazine’s error-filled story about flying, then turns the page and accepts its article on the economy without question.
fix: If a source is unreliable on the topics you can check, lower your trust in it on the topics you can’t.
note: Named by author Michael Crichton in a 2002 talk, after he once discussed the idea with physicist Murray Gell-Mann.

tests.s: Aisha, a nurse, spots several medical mistakes in a TV news segment, but she keeps relying on the same channel’s reports about other countries as if they were flawless.
A software engineer complains that a newspaper never gets technology stories right, then shares that paper’s article on nutrition as settled fact.

def: a short, familiar saying used to end a discussion or quiet doubts, instead of answering the actual point
scenario: When Liam asks why the team keeps missing deadlines, his manager says, “It is what it is,” and moves on to the next topic.
fix: When a slogan shuts down a question, ask the question again and request a real reason.
note: The term was popularized by psychiatrist Robert Jay Lifton in his 1961 book on “thought reform,” or brainwashing.

tests.s: Fatima asks the leader of her investment group why they should trust a risky scheme, and he only answers, “Don’t overthink it. Everything happens for a reason.”
Whenever a new volunteer questions how the group spends its money, the others just reply, “Trust the process,” and nobody explains anything further.

def: the habit of relying too much on a familiar tool or method, using it even for problems it does not suit
scenario: Having just learned spreadsheets, Kwame tries to use one to plan his wedding, write his toast and design the invitations.
fix: Before reaching for your favorite method, ask what the problem actually needs and what other tools could handle it better.
note: Philosopher Abraham Kaplan described it in 1964; Abraham Maslow’s 1966 version, about treating everything as a nail when your only tool is a hammer, is the best known.

tests.s: A consultant who built his career on cost-cutting recommends layoffs to every client, even a company whose real problem is that its product is out of date.
A data team that just bought a costly machine-learning system starts using it for every question, even ones a simple count would answer better.

def: the tendency to see the biases in other people’s judgments while believing your own judgment is fair and objective
scenario: Yuki reads about how ads sway shoppers and agrees most people are fooled, but she’s sure her own purchases are based only on quality.
fix: Assume the same biases you see in others probably affect you too, and use checks like blind reviews that don’t depend on judging yourself.
note: Named by psychologist Emily Pronin and colleagues in a 2002 paper.

tests.s: Every judge on a cooking-contest panel says the other judges favored contestants they knew, but each insists that their own scores were completely neutral.
Jamal explains that most people’s views on politics simply come from how they were raised, but he believes his own views come purely from careful study of the facts.

def: the tendency to judge harm caused by doing something as worse than equal or greater harm caused by doing nothing
scenario: Some parents who hear that a vaccine carries a tiny risk decide not to vaccinate, though the disease it prevents is far more dangerous.
fix: Compare the full results of acting and of not acting; choosing to do nothing is a choice too.
note: A 1990 study by Ilana Ritov and Jonathan Baron found people reluctant to vaccinate even when the disease was much deadlier than the vaccine.

tests.s: A town blames an official who approved a bridge repair that led to one accident far more harshly than an official who refused to fix another bridge that later collapsed and hurt many people.
A doctor avoids prescribing a drug with a small risk of side effects, accepting a much larger risk from the untreated illness because then, she says, “at least I didn’t cause it.”

def: the tendency to like something more simply because you have seen or heard it many times
scenario: Diego disliked a pop song the first time he heard it, but after hearing it on the radio every day for a month, it became one of his favorites.
fix: Ask whether you prefer something for its qualities or only because it feels familiar.
note: Psychologist Robert Zajonc published a key study of it in 1968.

tests.s: Olga thought a new building downtown was ugly when it opened, but after walking past it daily for a year, she now finds it rather handsome, though nothing about it has changed.
Shown a set of unfamiliar logos, people rate the ones they had glimpsed several times earlier as more pleasing than ones they had never seen.

def: a change in preference between two options when a third, clearly worse option is added to make one of them look better
scenario: A theater sells small popcorn for $3 and large for $7, and most people buy small. When it adds a medium for $6.50, most people switch to the large.
fix: Remove the option you would never pick and see whether your choice between the others still holds.

tests.s: A magazine offers online-only for $59 and print-plus-online for $125, and most readers pick online-only. After it adds a print-only option, also for $125, most choose print-plus-online.
A realtor shows Maria two homes she likes about equally, then a third that is like the first but costs more and needs a new roof. Suddenly Maria feels sure the first home is the best.

def: valuing something more just because you own it, so you ask more to sell it than you would pay to buy it
scenario: Hannah won’t sell the concert poster she was given for less than $40, yet she would never have paid more than $15 for the same poster in a shop.
fix: Ask what you would pay to get the item if you didn’t already have it; that is closer to its real value to you.
note: Economist Richard Thaler coined the term in 1980.

tests.s: Kwame was given a bottle of wine and turns down $50 for it, though he admits he would never spend more than $20 on that wine.
Office workers handed free company mugs ask far more to give them up than their coworkers without mugs will offer for the very same mug.

def: the tendency to give rewards and costs that come right now much more weight than ones that come later, even larger ones
scenario: Offered $50 today or $60 in a month, Jamal takes the $50, yet he would choose $60 in thirteen months over $50 in twelve.
fix: Picture the choice as if both options were far in the future; if your answer changes, the nearness of one option is swaying you.

tests.s: Each January, Priya plans to start saving for retirement “next month,” but every month she spends that money on things she wants right away.
Asked on Monday, most gym members say they’ll choose a workout over sleeping in on Saturday, but when Saturday morning comes, most of them stay in bed.

def: when a researcher’s hopes, without meaning to, change how people in a study act or how results are recorded
scenario: A researcher who expects a new teaching method to work smiles and nods more at the students using it, and those students try harder on the test.
fix: Keep the people running a study unaware of which group is which, so their expectations can’t shape the results.
note: Classic case: the horse Clever Hans seemed to do arithmetic until Oskar Pfungst showed in 1907 that it was reading its questioners’ unconscious cues.

tests.s: A horse seems to count by tapping its hoof, but it gets answers right only when its questioner knows the answer and, without meaning to, relaxes as the horse reaches the right number.
Tasters prefer a chef’s new sauce when he serves it himself, sure that it’s better, but when an assistant who doesn’t know which sauce is which serves them, the preference disappears.

def: the mistaken pattern: A or B is true; A is true; so B must be false, even though both could be true
scenario: “The job requires a degree or five years of experience. Sofia has a degree, so she must not have five years of experience.”
fix: Check whether “or” allows both options to be true; usually it does, so one being true tells you nothing about the other.

tests.s: “To get into the lounge, you need a gold card or a first-class ticket. Yuki has a gold card, so she can’t have a first-class ticket.”
“You get the discount if you’re a student or a senior. Liam is a student, so he can’t be a senior.”

def: an argument that, if it worked, would also prove things that are clearly false, which shows something is wrong with it
scenario: Omar argues that homework should be banned because some students find it stressful. By that logic, exams, sports tryouts and job interviews should all be banned too.
fix: Apply the same reasoning to other cases; if it leads to absurd conclusions there, it is flawed here too.

tests.s: “Cars should be banned because people sometimes die in accidents,” Ana argues, though the same reasoning would also ban stairs, swimming pools and kitchen knives.
A student claims that since memories can be wrong, no eyewitness should ever be believed, an argument that would also rule out trusting his own memory of the study he is citing.

def: assuming an outcome had just one cause when several causes worked together to produce it
scenario: After a losing season, fans blame only the new coach, ignoring injuries to three starting players and a much tougher schedule.
fix: List all the factors that could have contributed, and ask how much each one likely mattered.

tests.s: A news report blames a bridge collapse entirely on one overloaded truck, without mentioning years of skipped repairs and a flaw in the bridge’s design.
Wei insists his restaurant closed only because of one bad online review, though his rent had doubled and a new highway had moved traffic away from his street.

def: trying to turn an audience against someone before they speak, so that nothing the person says will be taken seriously
scenario: Before Maria presents her budget plan, a coworker tells the room, “Keep in mind she’s always been bad with numbers.”
fix: Judge what the person actually says when they say it, not the warning someone gave beforehand.
note: A personal attack made in advance. The phrase in this sense comes from John Henry Newman’s 1864 book Apologia Pro Vita Sua.

tests.s: Introducing the next debater, the host says, “Our next speaker will probably just repeat the usual nonsense, but let’s hear him out anyway.”
Before the new manager’s first meeting, Kofi tells his teammates that she’ll only pretend to listen and that any idea she brings will be useless.

def: the uncomfortable feeling of holding two beliefs that clash, or of acting against a belief, often eased by changing the belief
scenario: Liam sees himself as a healthy person but smokes every day, so he starts telling himself that a few cigarettes aren’t really harmful.
fix: When you notice yourself changing a belief right after acting against it, ask whether the evidence changed or only your comfort did.
note: The theory was proposed by psychologist Leon Festinger in 1957.

tests.s: Members of a group that predicted the world would end on a certain date become even more devoted after the date passes, saying their faith is what saved the world.
Rafael always said cheating is wrong, but after copying a classmate’s homework, he decides that homework rules are silly and copying isn’t really cheating.

def: spending far too much time on small, easy matters while large, complicated ones get little attention
scenario: A school board approves a $5 million building budget in ten minutes, then argues for an hour about the color of the new sign out front.
fix: Give each item time in proportion to how much it matters, and save the longest discussion for the biggest decisions.
note: Comes from C. Northcote Parkinson’s 1957 example of a committee that quickly approves a nuclear reactor but argues at length over a bicycle shed.

tests.s: A software team’s review skims the security setup in five minutes but spends an hour debating which shade of blue the login button should be.
At the condo meeting, owners approve a costly roof replacement almost at once, then argue for most of the evening about where to put the new bike rack.

q: cygnet : swan :: leveret : ?
why: A cygnet is a young swan, and a leveret is a young hare. A young rabbit is called a kit or kitten, so rabbit is the tempting wrong choice.

q: codicil : will :: amendment : ?
why: A codicil is a later addition that changes a will; an amendment is a later addition that changes a constitution. A legislature may pass amendments, but it is not the document being changed.

q: teetotaler : alcohol :: vegan : ?
why: A teetotaler never drinks alcohol, and a vegan never eats or uses animal products. Vegetables are what a vegan does eat, the reverse of the relationship.

q: plagiarize : ideas :: embezzle : ?
why: To plagiarize is to steal someone else’s ideas or words; to embezzle is to steal money you were trusted to manage. A bank is a place it might happen, not the thing taken.

q: stanza : poem :: movement : ?
why: A stanza is one section of a poem, and a movement is one section of a symphony. An orchestra performs the symphony but is not made of movements.

q: cacophony : sound :: eyesore : ?
why: A cacophony is a harsh, unpleasant sound, and an eyesore is an ugly, unpleasant sight. Noise belongs with the first pair, not the second.

q: heretic : religious doctrine :: dissident : ?
why: A heretic openly rejects the official teaching of a religion; a dissident openly opposes the official policy of a government. Prison may be a dissident’s fate, not what they reject.

q: invulnerable : harm :: infallible : ?
why: Something invulnerable cannot be harmed, and someone infallible cannot make an error. Criticism is tempting, but an infallible person can still be criticized; they just are never wrong.

q: pedant : minor details :: hypochondriac : ?
why: A pedant worries too much about minor details, and a hypochondriac worries too much about having an illness. Doctors are people a hypochondriac visits, not what they fret about.

q: anesthetic : pain :: muffler : ?
why: An anesthetic blocks or dulls pain, and a muffler dulls an engine’s noise. Exhaust passes through a muffler, but the muffler’s job is to quiet the noise, not to stop the exhaust.

q: frugality : extravagance :: diligence : ?
why: Frugality (careful spending) is the opposite of extravagance (wasteful spending), and diligence (steady hard work) is the opposite of laziness. Effort and care are close to diligence, not opposite.

q: drought : famine :: spark : ?
why: A drought can cause a famine, and a spark can cause a fire. Flint and a match produce sparks, so they come before the spark rather than after it.

q: “The dinner began with friendly persiflage about Tomás’s terrible golf swing, but the mood turned serious once the talk shifted to the layoffs.” What does persiflage most likely mean?
options: a toast given in honor of someone
why: It is friendly and about a golf swing, and it contrasts with the serious talk that follows, so it means playful joking. A heated argument would not be described as friendly.

q: “The judge fined the contumacious witness after he refused, for the third time, to answer her questions or obey her orders to stop interrupting.” What does contumacious most likely mean?
why: He refuses again and again to follow the judge’s orders, so the word means stubbornly refusing to obey authority. Nothing suggests he was nervous; his refusals were deliberate.

q: “The editor cut the paragraph as otiose: it repeated points already made, added no new facts, and served no purpose in the story.” What does otiose most likely mean?
why: The paragraph only repeated earlier points and “served no purpose,” so the word means useless or unnecessary. It is not called wrong or confusing, only pointless.

q: “The guard dog gave a low, minatory growl, and the delivery driver backed slowly toward the gate.” What does minatory most likely mean?
why: The growl makes the driver back away, so it is threatening. Playful would not make someone retreat, and the similar-looking word “minute” (tiny) is a trap.

q: “Health officials had declared the outbreak over, so the recrudescence of cases in the spring caught them off guard.” What does recrudescence most likely mean?
options: a fresh outbreak after a quiet period
why: The outbreak was thought to be over, then cases appeared again, so the word means breaking out again after a lull. A disappearance is the opposite of what surprised the officials.

q: “Many friendships begin through simple propinquity: people who sit near each other at work or live on the same hall tend to become close.” What does propinquity most likely mean?
why: The examples are sitting near each other and living on the same hall, so the word means being physically close. Shared hobbies could also start friendships, but the sentence’s examples are all about location.

q: “Instead of answering the reporter’s simple question, the senator began to bloviate, talking for ten minutes in grand phrases that said almost nothing.” What does bloviate most likely mean?
options: to speak at length in a pompous, empty way
why: He talks for ten minutes in grand phrases that say almost nothing, so the word means to speak long-windedly and pompously. Refusing to speak is the opposite of what he does.

q: “The coach’s hortatory halftime speech, full of calls to ‘dig deeper’ and ‘leave everything on the field,’ fired up the tired players.” What does hortatory most likely mean?
why: The speech is full of calls to try harder and it fires the players up, so it means urging people to act. Nothing in it is described as angry or insulting.

q: “After the scandal, the once-admired mayor faced months of public obloquy, with newspapers and former allies condemning her in harsh terms.” What does obloquy most likely mean?
why: She is condemned harshly by newspapers and former allies, so the word means fierce public criticism and the shame that follows. Praise and support is the opposite.

q: “Street vendors importuned the tourists at every corner, following them and asking again and again until the visitors finally bought something.” What does importune most likely mean?
options: to ask someone persistently and annoyingly
why: The vendors follow the tourists and ask again and again, so the word means to pester with repeated requests. “Bring goods from abroad” comes from confusing it with “import.”

q: “After years of saving, Aisha booked a sybaritic week at a resort: silk sheets, daily massages, and champagne at every sunset.” What does sybaritic most likely mean?
why: Silk sheets, massages and champagne describe indulgence and comfort, so the word means given over to luxury and pleasure. Simple and strict is the opposite.

q: “Unwilling to approve or reject the plan, the director chose to temporize, asking for more studies and putting off the vote month after month.” What does temporize most likely mean?
options: to stall in order to avoid deciding
why: The director avoids saying yes or no and keeps delaying with requests for studies, so the word means to stall to gain time. Acting boldly is the opposite of what the director does.

q: At an online store, the share of orders that were returned rose from 4% last year to 6% this year. Which must be true?
options: The return rate rose by 2 percentage points, a 50% increase in the rate.
The number of returned orders rose by 50%.
Twice as many orders were returned this year.
The store sold fewer items this year.
Customers were less happy this year.
why: Going from 4% to 6% is a rise of 2 percentage points, or 50% of the old rate, so “rose by 2%” is wrong. The number of returns is unknown, since total orders aren’t given.

term: Inference: speed bumps on worst streets
q: A city added speed bumps to the 10 streets that had the most crashes last year. This year, crashes on those 10 streets fell by 30%. Which, if true, most weakens the claim that the speed bumps caused the drop?
options: The speed bumps cost more than the city expected.
Drivers complained that the bumps slowed their trips.
Crashes on the city’s other streets stayed about the same.
In past years, streets that had unusually many crashes saw them fall by about 30% the next year even without any changes.
The bumps were painted bright yellow so drivers would see them.
Most of the crashes happened at night.
why: Streets picked for an unusually bad year tend to drift back toward normal on their own, so a 30% drop is what would be expected anyway. Steady crash rates on other streets would, if anything, support the bumps.

q: Patients taking a certain heart drug are more likely to die within a year than patients with heart disease who don’t take it. Which, if true, best explains this without the drug causing harm?
options: The drug must be taken twice a day.
Patients taking the drug see their doctors more often.
Some patients forget to take the drug.
The drug was approved only a few years ago.
Doctors mainly prescribe the drug to patients whose heart disease is already severe.
why: If the sickest patients are the ones who get the drug, they would die more often even if the drug helps. Missed doses might weaken the drug’s effect but would not make users die more than nonusers.

q: A shop’s owner says, “Our new website brought in more business: since it launched, online orders have doubled.” The argument depends on which assumption?
options: The website was cheap to build.
The growth in online orders did not come mostly from customers who used to order by phone or in person switching to the web.
Online customers spend more per order than other customers.
The shop’s competitors have no websites.
The website will keep working without problems.
Most of the shop’s customers are young.
why: If the extra online orders were just old customers changing how they order, total business may not have grown at all. Spending more per order is not needed for the owner’s claim.

q: A magazine asked readers to mail in their views on a new law. Of the 5,000 replies, 80% opposed it. The editors conclude that most people in the country oppose the law. What is the biggest weakness in this reasoning?
options: 5,000 replies is too few to say anything at all.
80% is not a large enough majority.
Some replies may have arrived late.
The law may change in the future.
The people who chose to reply, all readers of one magazine, may not think like the country as a whole.
The magazine did not say who wrote the law.
why: The replies come from self-selected readers of one magazine, who may feel more strongly or differently than others. A well-chosen sample of 5,000 would be plenty, so the size is not the main problem.

q: Over five years, a drug lowers the risk of a heart attack from 2 in 1,000 people to 1 in 1,000. An ad says the drug “cuts your risk in half.” Which is best supported?
options: Half of the people who take the drug will avoid a heart attack.
About 1,000 people would need to take the drug for five years to prevent one heart attack.
The drug lowers risk by 50 percentage points.
Without the drug, most people will have a heart attack.
The drug prevents 500 heart attacks per 1,000 users.
why: The risk falls by 1 in 1,000, so about 1,000 people must take it to prevent one heart attack. The ad is technically true, since 1 is half of 2, but it hides how small the change is.

term: Inference: air filters and sick days
q: After a factory installed new air filters, workers’ sick days fell by 20% over the next year. Which, if true, most strengthens the claim that the filters caused the drop?
options: Workers said they liked the new filters.
The filters cost less than expected.
Sick days also fell by about 20% at most other factories in the region that year.
The factory hired more workers that year.
At the company’s other factory nearby, which got no new filters, sick days stayed the same that year.
The filters must be replaced every six months.
why: A similar factory without filters showed no change, which helps rule out a general cause such as a mild flu season. A region-wide drop would weaken the claim, not strengthen it.

q: Corals get most of their food from tiny algae that live inside them. When the water stays too warm for weeks, corals push out the algae and turn white, which is called bleaching. Bleached corals can recover if the water cools soon enough, but if the algae don’t return, the coral starves. Which is best supported?
options: A coral that has bleached is not necessarily dead.
Cold water is the main cause of bleaching.
The algae harm the coral they live in.
Corals get all of their food from algae.
Warm water helps the algae grow inside corals.
why: The passage says bleached corals can recover if the water cools soon enough, so bleaching does not always mean death. It says “most” of their food comes from the algae, not all.

q: Class A has 20 students, whose average test score was 80. Class B has 30 students, whose average was 70. What was the average score of all 50 students together?
why: The total is 20 × 80 + 30 × 70 = 1,600 + 2,100 = 3,700, and 3,700 ÷ 50 = 74. Simply averaging 80 and 70 gives 75, which ignores that Class B is larger.

q: A report finds that most car crashes happen within five miles of the driver’s home and concludes that driving near home is more dangerous than driving farther away. Which best explains the finding without that conclusion being true?
options: Roads near homes have more stop signs.
Crash reports are often filed late.
Drivers far from home use maps.
Most of the driving people do is within a few miles of home.
why: If most miles are driven near home, most crashes would happen there even if each mile is no riskier. Faster highway driving would, if anything, make far-from-home driving look more dangerous.

q: A town has 10,000 registered voters. In a recent election, 60% of them voted, and Candidate Reyes won 55% of the votes cast. Each voter cast one vote in this race. Which must be true?
options: Most of the town’s registered voters voted for Reyes.
Reyes received votes from 55% of the registered voters.
why: 6,000 people voted, and 55% of 6,000 is 3,300. The 5,500 figure wrongly applies 55% to all 10,000 registered voters, most of whom did not vote for Reyes.

q: Trees in cool climates usually add one growth ring each year, wider in good growing years and narrower in poor ones. The pattern of rings in a beam from an old barn exactly matches part of a dated record from local trees, and the beam’s outermost ring matches the year 1842. Which is best supported?
options: The tree was cut down before 1842.
The summer of 1842 was very dry.
The tree that the beam came from was still alive in 1842.
Every tree in the world adds exactly one ring per year.
why: A ring for 1842 means the tree was still growing that year. The barn need not date from 1842, since outer rings may have been trimmed off and the barn could have been built later.

q: Five people live on floors 1 to 5 of a building, one per floor. Dee lives on the floor directly above Ana. Eli lives below Bo, and Bo lives below Caz. Ana does not live on floor 1. Caz does not live on the top floor. Who lives on floor 3?
why: If Ana and Dee were on floors 2–3 or 3–4, Caz, the highest of Eli, Bo and Caz, would land on floor 5, which is not allowed. So Ana and Dee are on 4 and 5, and Eli, Bo and Caz fill floors 1, 2 and 3.

term: Logic: not the case that none
q: “It is not the case that none of the applicants speak French.” Which statement means the same?
options: All of the applicants speak French.
Most of the applicants speak French.
At least one applicant speaks French.
At least one applicant does not speak French.
why: Denying “none speak French” means at least one does. It doesn’t tell us that all, most or exactly one do, and it says nothing about whether anyone doesn’t.

q: Tara will join the trip only if Uri joins. Uri joins whenever the trip falls on a weekend. Tara joined the trip. Which must be true?
options: Uri joined, and the trip was on a weekend.
Nothing can be concluded about Uri.
The trip was on a weekday.
Uri may or may not have joined.
Whenever Uri joins, Tara joins too.
Uri joined, but the trip may not have been on a weekend.
why: Tara joining requires Uri, so Uri joined. A weekend guarantees Uri joins, but Uri might join on other days too, so we can’t tell when the trip was.

q: No reptiles have fur. Some pets have fur. Which must be true?
options: Every pet with fur is a dog or a cat.
why: The pets that have fur can’t be reptiles, so at least some pets are not reptiles. Nothing rules out other pets being reptiles, so “No pets are reptiles” does not follow.

q: Three boxes are labeled “Apples,” “Oranges” and “Mixed.” One holds only apples, one only oranges, and one both, but every label is wrong. You take one fruit from the box labeled “Mixed,” and it is an apple. What is in the box labeled “Oranges”?
options: Either only apples or only oranges
why: The “Mixed” box can’t really be mixed, so the apple shows it holds only apples. The “Oranges” box can’t hold oranges, and apples are taken, so it holds the mix.

q: Of 100 employees, 80 drink coffee, 70 drink tea and 60 drink juice. What is the smallest possible number who drink all three?
why: At most 20 skip coffee, 30 skip tea and 40 skip juice, so at most 90 people skip at least one drink. That leaves at least 10 who drink all three, and 10 is possible if no one skips two drinks.

q: Any student who earns all A’s makes the honor roll. A student makes the honor roll only if she has five or fewer absences. Ines earned all A’s. Which must be true?
options: Ines may have more than five absences.
Every student with five or fewer absences makes the honor roll.
Only students with all A’s make the honor roll.
Ines did not make the honor roll.
Ines has five or fewer absences.
Ines made the honor roll, but her absences can’t be judged.
why: All A’s puts Ines on the honor roll, and being on the honor roll requires five or fewer absences. “Every student with five or fewer absences makes the honor roll” reverses the “only if” rule and is not stated.

q: If the shop is open, then Ali or Bea is working. Bea works only on weekends. Today is Tuesday, and Ali is home sick and not working. Which must be true?
options: The shop is open, but no one is working.
why: Bea can’t work on a Tuesday and Ali isn’t working, so neither is working. An open shop would need one of them, so the shop is closed.

q: Which statement means the same as “Neither Jo nor Kim was at the party”?
options: Jo or Kim was not at the party.
Jo and Kim were not both at the party.
Jo was not at the party, and Kim was not at the party.
Jo was at the party, but Kim was not.
At least one of them was at the party.
If Jo was at the party, Kim was not.
why: “Neither…nor” means both were absent. “Not both were there” is weaker: it would still be true if one of them came.

q: Most of a club’s members are students. Most of the club’s members are under 25. Which must be true?
options: Most students in the club are under 25.
All students in the club are under 25.
Exactly half the members are students.
No member is both a student and under 25.
At least one member is both a student and under 25.
why: Each group is more than half the club, so the two groups must overlap in at least one person. They could overlap only slightly, so “most students are under 25” does not follow.

q: Ari, Ben, Cam and Dov each ordered a different drink: tea, coffee, juice or cocoa. Ari ordered neither tea nor coffee. Ben ordered either cocoa or juice. Cam did not order tea. Which must be true?
why: Ari and Ben use up juice and cocoa between them, though we can’t tell who has which. That leaves tea and coffee for Cam and Dov, and since Cam didn’t order tea, Dov did.

term: Logic: light if and only if
q: The light is on if and only if the switch is up and the power is on. Right now the light is off, and the switch is up. Which must be true?
options: Both the switch and the power are off.
why: With “if and only if,” the light is off exactly when at least one condition fails. The switch is up, so the power must be off. The rule as stated leaves no room for other causes, such as a burned-out bulb.

q: Which word is most similar in meaning to perspicuous (as in “a perspicuous explanation”)?
why: Perspicuous means clearly expressed and easy to understand. Insightful is the meaning of perspicacious, a different word that looks very similar.

q: Which word is most nearly the OPPOSITE of tenebrous?
why: Tenebrous means dark and shadowy, so luminous (full of light) is its opposite. Shadowy and gloomy are close in meaning, not opposite.

q: Which word is most similar in meaning to expatiate (as in “expatiate on a topic”)?
why: To expatiate is to speak or write about something at length and in detail, which is to elaborate. Emigrate comes from confusing it with “expatriate.”

q: Which word is most nearly the OPPOSITE of laudatory (as in “a laudatory review”)?
why: Laudatory means expressing praise, so condemning is its opposite. Praising and approving mean nearly the same as laudatory.

q: Which word is the odd one out? obstinate, intransigent, obdurate, adamant, recalcitrant, pliant
why: The other five all describe someone who refuses to change their mind or give way. Pliant means easily bent or persuaded, the opposite.

q: Which word is the odd one out? sonnet, haiku, limerick, villanelle, ode, novella
why: Sonnets, haiku, limericks, villanelles and odes are all kinds of poems. A novella is a short novel, written in prose.

q: Which word is the odd one out? telescope, microscope, periscope, stethoscope, kaleidoscope, horoscope
why: All the others are instruments for looking or, in the stethoscope’s case, listening. A horoscope is not a device but a forecast that astrologers base on the positions of the sun, moon and planets.

q: Which pair does NOT show the same relationship as the others?
why: In every other pair, the first word is the young of the animal. A drake is an adult male duck, not a baby one; a young duck is a duckling.

q: Which word is most similar in meaning to inimical (as in “habits inimical to good health”)?
why: Inimical means harmful or working against something. Unique is the trap: it is close to inimitable, a different word that looks similar.

q: Which word is most nearly the OPPOSITE of diffident?
why: Diffident means shy and lacking confidence, so confident is its opposite. Shy is a synonym, and different only sounds similar.

q: Which word is the odd one out? corroborate, substantiate, confirm, verify, validate, refute
why: The other five all mean showing that something is true. To refute is to show that something is false.

q: Which pair does NOT show the same relationship as the others?
why: Each other instrument measures the amount of the thing named. A telescope lets you see faraway objects like stars but doesn’t measure them.

def: a pattern that shows up in every smaller group within the data but reverses when all the groups are combined into one
scenario: Treatment A works better than Treatment B for small kidney stones and also for large ones, yet B looks better overall, because A was used mostly on the harder, large stones.
fix: Before trusting a combined rate, check whether the groups being compared contain very different mixes of easy and hard cases.
note: Named for statistician Edward H. Simpson, who described it in 1951; Karl Pearson and Udny Yule had noted similar effects earlier.

tests.s: In each half of the season, Diego had a higher batting average than Malik, yet Malik’s average for the whole season was higher, because Diego got most of his at-bats in the half when everyone hit poorly.

In each of a college’s two departments, women were admitted at a higher rate than men, but overall the college admitted a smaller share of women, because most women applied to the department that turned away most applicants.

def: starting from how likely something seemed at first, then adjusting that belief by how strongly each new piece of evidence points one way
scenario: Hannah thinks there is about a 1 in 4 chance her flight will be delayed. When she learns a major storm is moving in, she raises her estimate to about even odds instead of jumping straight to certainty.
fix: Ask two questions: how likely was this before the evidence, and how much more likely is this evidence if the claim is true than if it is false?
note: A method, not a mistake: it avoids both ignoring the starting odds (base rate neglect) and ignoring the new evidence.

tests.s: A doctor first thinks a rash is most likely an allergy. When a fever appears, which is common with infections but rare with allergies, she shifts toward infection while still keeping allergy in mind.
Yuki puts a 20% chance on a rumor about her company being true. When a reliable reporter confirms part of it, she raises her estimate to about 60%, not all the way to 100%.

def: trying many different ways of analyzing data until one gives a “statistically significant” result, then reporting only that one
scenario: A researcher finds no link between coffee and test scores, so she splits the data by age, gender, time of day and type of coffee until one subgroup shows a significant result, and publishes just that.
fix: Trust studies that announced their exact analysis plan before collecting data, and ask how many comparisons were tried in total.
